Engine Integration and testing – demonstration on AJAX 2802 ULE and Cummins X15N engines to quantify methane slip reductions. 1.3 Key Results  Bench-scale tests confirmed linear hydrogen generation of 0.075 percent per watt of plasma power with an approximate energy consumption of 74 kJ/mol of converted methane, which is in-line with theoretical predictions for the following methane decomposition reaction, CH → C + H (H° = 74.8 kJ/mol). 4 2  High-flow testing demonstrated stable operation through 300 SLPM and defined the upper limit of plasma stability.  AJAX engine tests showed 1–2 percent methane reduction at 400 W (0.13 % of engine output), with reduced VOCs and NO levels. x  Cummins X15N tests produced 6–27 percent methane reduction at 600 W (0.25 % of engine output). All performance objectives were achieved while maintaining plasma power consumption below one percent of the total engine power level. 1.4 Challenges and Resolutions During development, several technical issues were identified and resolved to ensure stable operation. Electrical arcing within the gas-delivery section was eliminated by adding dielectric insulation and repairing the affected power delivery channel. Thermal overload in the pulse-power module was mitigated by paralleling switching transistors, improving air cooling, and refining temperature interlock settings. Electrical noise is a characteristic feature of pulsed plasmas and sufficient grounding and/or shielding was essential to minimize the impact of electromagnetic interference (EMI) on engine controls or analytical systems. Minor insulator surface melting from capacitive charge buildup was prevented by redesigning the high-voltage connector and removing redundant insulation. These modifications resulted in improved reformer reliability with fewer thermal faults. Southwest Research Institute® U.S. DOE Award Number DE-FE0032301 Public Version - 1 - DE-FE0032301 Final Report 1.5 Impact and Outcomes The project validated an energy-efficient approach to reduce methane slip for legacy natural-gas engines. It advanced the technology to TRL 5 and generated an invention disclosure entitled “Low- Cost Electrical System for Generating High-Voltage Pulsed DC Output for Plasma Generation.” The reformer’s retrofit compatibility, modular design, and minimal power draw align directly with DOE’s Methane-Reduction Program goals. Follow-on activities are currently underway with industry partners to further mature the technology to enable future field testing. SECTION 2 — Background, Objectives, and Methodology 2.1 Background and Rationale Methane (CH ) is a short-lived but potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential more 4 than twenty times that of carbon dioxide on a 100-year basis. Within the natural-gas value chain, combustion slip from compressor engines is a major contributor to methane leaks. Even modern ultra-low-emission (ULE) engines can release 2‒8g CH /bhp-hr (break horsepower hour), while 4 legacy equipment often exceeds 15g CH /bhp-hr.
